Peta's Angora video: Truth or fabrication?

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: Angora goats are known for their exotic hair but in a recent video by an animal rights organisation that shocked the world disturbing visuals of goats in distres

Unique Selling Point:
The video, produced by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or Peta, went viral on the 1st of May and since over 100 brands have threatened to stop using mohair in their clothing range.

Peta is the largest animal rights organisation in the world with 6.5 million members and supporters. Their top video this month on the angora practices in South Africa, is headlined: “PETA has decimated the angora industry. Now let’s win against mohair!.” In 2015 they destroyed the angora rabbit fur industry in China and their next target was the mohair industry in South Africa. In this 4 minute video produced by Peta they claim “goats are thrown, cut and killed for mohair,” and are calling on a total ban of all mohair products from South Africa. The message resonated strongly as already international brands like Zara, Gap, H&M, Mango, Topshop, Banana Republic, Esprit, Old Navy, Athleta have agreed to take all mohair products off their 2020 winter range. This could spell the end of the mohair industry for South Africa, the potential loss 30 000 jobs and a R1.5 billion rand industry closing down.

Peta promotes a total vegan lifestyle and say “animals are not ours to eat, wear, experiment on, use for entertainment or abuse in any way.” They are known to go to extreme lengths to create sensational news and often reported in the media as ‘getting their facts wrong.’ And on every news story where they feed on the emotions of the consumer, the ‘donate’ tab is in bold. Money speaks loudest and rumours has it that their biggest donors are from the oil companies. This has a twofold implication: promoting of synthetic fibres and secondly, an urban myth that the angora farms are smack back in the middle of the Karoo where fracking is said to take place. (our story will not cover these points as that will need far more investigation and possibly a follow up).


Summary:
According to Peta they visited 12 angora farms in the Karoo and “documented pervasive cruelty to animals at every single farm”. “Shearers threw angora goats; cut off swaths of their skin, and cut conscious animals’ throats. Workers picked up goats by the tails, likely breaking them. One farmer dumped rams into tanks of cleaning solution and shoved their heads into the liquid, which he admitted would poison them if they swallowed it.” They continue by saying: “workers punched holes in goats’ ears with pliers, causing the animals to scream.

There is no doubt that the visuals are highly disturbing to watch, but look deeper and every single scene has been explained to us in detail by experts on what is standard acceptable procedures and not harmful to the animals in any way as Peta claimed. Par for the one scene where the adult goats are being handled roughly by shearers who were obviously in a hurry to finish, the rest of the scenes are not ‘cruel to animals’ as they claimed. Most consumers have no first hand knowledge of farming practices passed by the NSPCA and independent auditors. Farmers work with strict guidelines on sustainable practices and are controlled by independent organisations like Mohair SA to regulate and monitor farmers. Angora goats are highly sensitive animals and a farmer will go out of his way to ensure that his animal is treated in the best way as this is his ‘bread and butter’.



Further information:
In February this year a Brit by the name of Joel Hindson, knocked on the door of the only estate agent in Steytlerville in the Karoo, posing as a potential buyer of a mohair farm. Linda Henderson, wife of a farmer and now an estate agent, knows the industry backwards and was eager to help this ‘lovely young man.’ She put him in touch with some of the top angora farmers in the area and further afield: farmers from Jansenville, Aberdeen, Prins Albert were all on the list who welcomed the young man into their homes and heart so to speak. Little did Linda know that Hindson’s intentions was far from being honorable.

Henderson spent 6 weeks in the Karoo as a guest on the farms using their hospitality, knowledge they shared and practices they showed him to manipulate the truth to suit his own end purpose.

Every single farmer will vouch for what happened on the farm and how Henderson has twisted the facts and used information out of context to weave a story of deceit.

On Dicky Ogilvy’s farm in the Aberdeen district near Graaff Reinet, Henderson were taken in as a guest for a week, eat their chops, and went around the farm asking many questions showing a fake interest in the ‘running of the farm’. On one day when Ogilvy had a meeting in town he left Henderson with the shearing team where the kids were being shorn for the first time. As Dicky will tell you, “the kids scream as they are like any child going for a hair cut for the first time which no child enjoys so they kick up a fuss for the first few times and then thereafter they become used to the shearing scissors and will lie still and sometimes even enjoy it”. He further explained why they are dragged by their legs as that is the best way to isolate a single one by picking it up amongst the group; secondly, kids are picked up that way in the first few days after being born to prevent the human scent on the animal as the mother will reject the kid if it she does not recognise the smell. The kids therefor get used to being picked up that way. It was during this time that Henderon took his undercover camera and filmed the kids screaming whilst being shorn for the first time.

The live goat being slaughtered was explained as a tradition in african culture and acceptable even to this day by the Animal Protection Act as not cruel. Ogilvy explained that shearers get a free goat for every 1000 they shear and in their tradition they they slaughter the goat with a ‘sharp’ knife (not blunt as per the Peta video) and share the meat amongst themselves and for their families.

On AB Dobson’s farm, the son Sean said his father was totally misquoted on a story told to Henderson of 40 000 goats that died during a fluke cold spell that hit the Karoo in the eighties when the goats were shorn and that night the weather turned to freezing cold. Most farmers lost thousands of angora goats as they could not predict the weather. (there were no Aps during those days). In the video Henderson claims 30 000 goats die as the norm due to cruelty of shearing these animals.

Guy van Hasselt, another farmer Henderson visited, will tell you that if you don't’ shear your goats, their hair will get knotted, too long and uncomfortable covering their eyes, and the kid won’t be able to find the teat. The dipping process is part of this prevention method to kill or lice, and rid the animal from unwanted feces clinging to the fur. The dipping liquid is an approved, quality control, goat friendly substance not harmfull in any way. The practice of dipping the head underwater is the same as ‘us washing our hair’ says Guy. If you don’t get to the head you have not done a thorough job and the lice will simply stay on.
Fred Colborne is from farmers stock of 150 years in the Willomore area. Colborne is ‘gutted’ by the whole thing. On his farm, Heindson secretly filmed the tattooing process claiming that it is cruel. Once again, there is an explanation. Colmore says, as with human ears being pierced, it is sensitive for the goat but the tools used are checked and the needles and pliers are standard equipment and the best method as it is a quick process and done by specialised instructors from the ram breeders association. A sharp sterilised needle is used to ensure no infection takes place. Throughout the ages, all animals are branded with the farmer’s initials and for stud animals they receive a special tattoo that will identify the owner during auction process.

The scene of the dead goat says Hasselt was simply an animal that died in the veld and only found after a couple of days. The farmers had extreme drought and as a result lost some animals.

In each of the video scenes no context was given, no expert advice was seeked, no industry leaders were asked to comment and no farmers were given the right to explain. The only step Peta took was to contact NSPCA and lodged a complaint. The NSPCA have confirmed that they have not found anything untoward but shearing process is still to be investigated as the season is past now.

The only scene in the video where strong action has been taken, is the adult goats that are being handled in a very rough way by the shearers. The particular farmer is a commercial farmer (Chris van Schalkwyk i was told) and has been put on suspension till the full investigation by an independent auditor from Mohair SA and the NSPCA has been completed. He is also banned from selling his angora fur on any auctions till further notice.

We will also investigate the team that was responsible for the rough handling of the adult goats and speak to the leader and an expert in the shearing business to ascertain what went wrong and how this could have happened in an industry where strict guidelines and procedures are followed. Shearers are all from Lesotho as they grow up in a family where there fathers were shearers and so it is passed on from generation to generation. Initially all youngsters are monitored until they qualify and are ready to work independently. The OVK or Oos Vrystaat Kaap is the leading organisation that is responsible for shearing teams and as Santa Ferreira from OVK says, we will find out who the shearers were and take the necessary steps against them as this is damaging for our whole industry. The farmers rely on us to provide them with the skilled labour and we cannot afford this to put the industry in disrepute.

Dr. Malcolm Hobson, an independent Vet appointed by the Mohair industry responsible for animal health and vet support might be a good call to interview regarding the footage he saw and his take on this.

Finally, Yolanda Taylor, Director of Corporate Projects for Peta, will be on skype for an on camera interview. Peta has given permission for the use of the video in our programme.

There is no need for Carte Blanche to go ‘undercover’ to get our own footage. As explained in all the scenes, most of what you saw is standard, ethical and sustainable practice. Henderson for example mention 12 farms. On only one farm did he manage to implicate cruel behaviour. Every other scene was manipulated. Guy van Hasselt from example, a very reputable farmer, were also visited by as there was nothing to show that wa untoward, no visuals were used.
The question we have to ask, are we prepared to see a whole industry folding due to a single incident that took place. The video is grossly unfair to the mohair farmers and the truth must prevail.

In our story we go to the farmers who were implicated in the video, the shearers (as they work for independent companies) the organisations representing the industry and the animal welfare organisations. Peta will be on Skype to be questioned.

More information:
South Africa produces 60% of the world’s mohair with the remaining 40% produced in Texas, Australia, Lesotho and Spain. 95% of all mohair in the world is processed at factories in Port Elizabeth. Some of the yarn remain here for local products but most is bought by international buyers from Europe and Asia and makes its way to the shelves of top fashion retailers.

Press Release:


Mohair Goats
South Africa's Angora goat farmers are hotly disputing the validity of footage which allegedly shows their goats bleating in distress. In an already tenuous job market, a sensational video by an influential animal rights organisation is threatening to close down the mohair wool industry that has survived for over 150 years and ensures the livelihood of around 30,000 people in South Africa. The video has caused several big name fashion brands to withdraw their use of mohair leaving the farmers and the multi-million rand industry in dire straits. Carte Blanche examines the legitimacy of this infamous video.


Script:


Script: Angora goats
Duration: 10:10 Date: 28 June 2018
Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Derek Watts

V/O South Africa produces 60% of the world’s mohair. 3.8 Million tons of this luxury high end fibre is exported for international clothing brands to Europe, China and Taiwan. Nearly 1000 Angora farms producing mohair are found in a condensed area in the Karoo. A video of angora goats in distress during shearing, is now threatening to close down the industry and put 30 000 people out of a job.

Up sound

V/O The video was taken on angora farms in January, by an undercover animal rights agent from the UK. It shows goats being dragged across the floor by the legs or the horns; you hear the disturbing sounds of kid goats crying. It becomes simply unbearable to watch.

Up sound

LINK: The video was produced by a massive animal rights organisation, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or PETA, but now questions are being asked whether the video was ethically produced or indeed accurate.

V/O Peta is an international vegan organisation with 6.5 million members, known for its sensational animal anti-cruelty campaigns. South Africa’s mohair industry is its latest target. In 2015 Peta claimed victory after they ran a worldwide campaign against the angora rabbit farms in China. They stated: “Peta has decimated the angora industry! Now let’s win against mohair!”

LINK: The story starts in January this year when an Englishman by the name of Joel Hindson knocked on the door of the only estate agent in Steytlerville in the Karoo, posing as a potential buyer of an angora mohair farm.

V/O Linda Henderson put Hindson in touch with angora farmers in the area.

Linda Henderson: Estate Agent - He reported to be interested in angora goat farming and asked me if I could help him to find his way around farms. He was very particularly interested in the shearing.

V/O Sean Hobson is a sixth generation farmer from Jansenville.

Sean Hobson: Angora farmer – One of the industry players contacted us and said there is this young man from England who is looking to come to South Africa, buy a farm, start farming goats.

V/O During a shearing session Hindson secretly recorded a conversation around the table where Hobson’s father made reference to 40 000 goats that died after a freak weather change in the last century. Peta claimed many goats die of the cold after shearing.

Derek Watts: What is the part that is misquoted?

Sean Hobson: I was at the shearing table across the table form my dad: Joel was at my left and we were talking about the industry in the eighties, and at one stage there was a massive cold snap that hit the country straight after shearing season and a lot of animals were lost. My dad was talking about a very specific situation that happened 40 odd years ago and this guy quoted that this is something that happens on a regular basis, it’s a lie.

V/O Hindson became a familiar face in the area. He visited Fred Colborne from Willowmore during the branding of his goats.

Derek Watts: A lot of people are perturbed about the so-called tattooing process,

Fred Colborne: Angora farmer - Yeh the tattooing is law in our country and it is done annually once off on a goat at a time.

Derek Watts: Would you say there is a lot of suffering?

Fred Colborne: No, No, definitely not. If it is done correctly and the goats are handled properly, definitely not a lot of suffering at all.

V/O Hindson moved on to Dicky Ogilvy’s farm near Aberdeen. Ogilvy was shearing his goat kids at the time.

Derek Watts: Now the bleating of your kids is a big part of the video. How do you explain that?

Dicky Ogilvy: Angora farmer - A goat kid by nature, at that age 5,6 months old, they are bleaters of note. Inevitably like any young animal, they are scared. You will find at the second shearing they are dead quiet.

Up sound: Vet with Ogilvy looking at sheep with eye problem

V/O Macky Hobson is a vet from Graaff-Reinet who was appointed by the mohair industry to look after the welfare of the goats and do farm visits.

Derek Watts: It is claimed that the shearing process is incredibly cruel and painful.

Macky Hobson: Veterinarian - I totally disagree with that, the shearing process is an absolute necessity for angora goats. If you didn’t shear an angora goat these goats will suffer incredibly if they were not shorn.

V/O During Hindson’s visit to Ogilvy’s farm, a sick goat was slaughtered. Peta claimed it was done with a blunt knife.

Dicky Ogilvy: That particular case it was a goat that had a cancerous growth on her head, she was in huge discomfort and it was done in such a way as humanly as possible. It was not done with a blunt knife.

V/O Peta says that ‘goats who are unprofitable, die agonising deaths’. Farmers say goats are slaughtered only when they have lost their teeth and are unable to eat.

Up Peta video; goat being dragged by legs.

Derek Watts: What about dragging the goats around by their legs?

Mackie Hobson: Look Derek that is not the norm and it is unacceptable and certainly those shearing teams the whole welfare of those shearing teams, those people need to be trained.

V/O Shearing is done by outside contractors: OVK is the largest in southern Africa with 900 shearers who pay their workers per goat they shear. Graham Frost manages the shearing teams.

Derek Watts: It is a very rushed operation which I guess is tied in with salaries and bonuses, is there not a way to actually give them more time to shear the goats?

Graham Frost: Manager Shearing Services OVK - I quite agree they are probably racing for the fact of getting as much money as they can as quickly as they can and I think we must look into it.

Derek Watts: We see a shearer actually sitting on a goat?

Graham Frost: I am very distressed that that actually happened and we must get to the actual fact what happened. Certainly it is not in our practice to do that.

Derek Watts: But in the video we see a goat being pulled by the leg.

Graham Frost: It is definitely an issue which I will strictly address with people concerned.

V/O Mohair SA, the regulating body for the industry, conducted an internal investigation on the two farms and the OVK shearing teams implicated in the Peta video. OVK said once it has identified the shearers on the video it will suspend their contracts if they are found guilty. The two implicated farmers have been suspended; one of them was Ogilvy.

Derek Watts: What were your thoughts when you saw the Peta video?

Dicky Ogilvy: I was shocked. Initially I didn't even think this guy could have done this and then having a better look at it I realised I have been implicated here. What went down on that video was edited and narrated in such a way to discredit the entire industry which is grossly unfair.

V/O Deon Saayman of Mohair SA is adamant that the scenes depicted in the video is not a true reflection of the mohair industry.

Deon Saayman: Managing Director Mohair SA: If you look at these two specific clips these are very isolated incidents Derek. We spent nearly a decade putting sustainable guidelines in place; we have nearly assessed 450 farmers to get on with these practices.

V/O An independent investigation by the National SPCA is now in progress. Grace de Lange from the Farm Animal Protection Unit says they will lay charges once they have concluded their findings.

Grace de Lange: Manager Farm Animal Protection Unit - We were horrified by some of the things we saw like the dragging of the animals by the legs and horns. So if the shearing company, the farmers and the individuals identified are found guilty of animal cruelty they will face heavy fines, imprisonment, and they will get a criminal record.

V/O Hindson visited 12 of the nearly 1000 angora farms in South Africa of which only two were implicated. We called Daniel Paden, Director of Evidence Analysis for PETA in USA.

Derek Watts: The point is you have made no attempt to produce a balanced video. You have not gone to anyone in the industry. You have not even gone to vets in this country.

Daniel Paden: Director of Evidence Analysis PETA USA: We consulted with no fewer than 6 vets in US and Uk and the consensus there, anonymous, is that what was depicted on that video cause those animals pain and suffering.

Derek Watts: Daniel your video is really riddled with inaccuracy, you say that 40 000 goats die a year because of the weather and shearing?

Daniel Paden: No the video shows a mohair farmer saying that on one weekend alone 40 000 goats die of exposure in South Africa.

Derek Watts: Now the truth there is that goes back to the last century that story and these days the farmers have weather apps to get their goats into enclosures when the weather closes in.

Derek Watts: Daniel, what now must happen to almost a million goats around SA?

Daniel Paden: My suspicion is that the farmers would probably start to slaughter them in various ways if the demand is going down and they find that they can no longer sell those animals fleeces.

V/O On Peta’s website they list over a hundred clothing brands who have joined the boycott against mohair form South Africa: Zara; H&M and Forever 21 is on that list.

Derek Watts: What would you say to the world leading brands considering dropping mohair from their ranges?

Sean Hobson: We are incredibly proud of our animals. Our animals are our livelihood. Look for the balanced story. Look for the truth out there.
__________________________________________________________________________

PROMOS
10 second
A video from an animal rights organisation that went viral, threatens to bring down 150 year old mohair industry and put 30 000 people out of a job.

15 second
V/O A video by an animal rights organisation of angora goats in distress threatens to close down the mohair industry.
Deon Saayman: the first time you see this video, immediately shock, outrage, anger

15 seconds
V/O A video of angora goats being apparently treated cruelly threatens to bring down a 150 year old mohair industry.
Sean Hobson: Our animals are our livelihood. Look for the balanced story. Look for the truth out there.

30 second
V/O A sensational video from an animal rights organisation showing disturbing images of angora goats being shorn for their mohair is threatening to close down the industry and 30 000 people out of a job.
Sean Hobson: My life is my goats. It's what i do, it is what my family has done for 6 generations. I can’t accept the fact that a group can shut down my livelihood off a sensationalistic video like that. It's what i do it's my passion.

SUNDAY PROMO
A video which shows alleged abuse on Angora mohair farms threatens a one hundred and fifty year old industry. Was this animal rights video, fair and balanced?

The kids therefor get used to being picked up that way. It was during this time that Henderon took his undercover camera and filmed the kids screaming whilst being shorn for the first time. The live goat being slaughtered was explained as a tradition in african culture and acceptable even to this day by the Animal Protection Act as not cruel. Ogilvy explained that shearers get a free goat for every 1000 they shear and in their tradition they they slaughter the goat with a ‘sharp’ knife (not blunt as per the Peta video) and share the meat amongst themselves and for their families. On AB Dobson’s farm, the son Sean said his father was totally misquoted on a story told to Henderson of 40 000 goats that died during a fluke cold spell that hit the Karoo in the eighties when the goats were shorn and that night the weather turned to freezing cold. The only step Peta took was to contact NSPCA and lodged a complaint. The NSPCA have confirmed that they have not found anything untoward but shearing process is still to be investigated as the season is past now. The only scene in the video where strong action has been taken, is the adult goats that are being handled in a very rough way by the shearers. The particular farmer is a commercial farmer (Chris van Schalkwyk i was told) and has been put on suspension till the full investigation by an independent auditor from Mohair SA and the NSPCA has been completed. He is also banned from selling his angora fur on any auctions till further notice. We will also investigate the team that was responsible for the rough handling of the adult goats and speak to the leader and an expert in the shearing business to ascertain what went wrong and how this could have happened in an industry where strict guidelines and procedures are followed. Shearers are all from Lesotho as they grow up in a family where there fathers were shearers and so it is passed on from generation to generation. Initially all youngsters are monitored until they qualify and are ready to work independently. The farmers rely on us to provide them with the skilled labour and we cannot afford this to put the industry in disrepute. Dr. Malcolm Hobson, an independent Vet appointed by the Mohair industry responsible for animal health and vet support might be a good call to interview regarding the footage he saw and his take on this. Finally, Yolanda Taylor, Director of Corporate Projects for Peta, will be on skype for an on camera interview. Peta has given permission for the use of the video in our programme. There is no need for Carte Blanche to go ‘undercover’ to get our own footage. As explained in all the scenes, most of what you saw is standard, ethical and sustainable practice. Henderson for example mention 12 farms. On only one farm did he manage to implicate cruel behaviour. Every other scene was manipulated. Guy van Hasselt from example, a very reputable farmer, were also visited by as there was nothing to show that wa untoward, no visuals were used. The question we have to ask, are we prepared to see a whole industry folding due to a single incident that took place. The video is grossly unfair to the mohair farmers and the truth must prevail. In our story we go to the farmers who were implicated in the video, the shearers (as they work for independent companies) the organisations representing the industry and the animal welfare organisations. Peta will be on Skype to be questioned. More information: South Africa produces 60% of the world’s mohair with the remaining 40% produced in Texas, Australia, Lesotho and Spain. 95% of all mohair in the world is processed at factories in Port Elizabeth. Some of the yarn remain here for local products but most is bought by international buyers from Europe and Asia and makes its way to the shelves of top fashion retailers. 2018 Press Release: Mohair Goats South Africa's Angora goat farmers are hotly disputing the validity of footage which allegedly shows their goats bleating in distress. In an already tenuous job market, a sensational video by an influential animal rights organisation is threatening to close down the mohair wool industry that has survived for over 150 years and ensures the livelihood of around 30,000 people in South Africa. The video has caused several big name fashion brands to withdraw their use of mohair leaving the farmers and the multi-million rand industry in dire straits. Carte Blanche examines the legitimacy of this infamous video. Script: Script: Angora goats Duration: 10:10 Date: 28 June 2018 Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Derek Watts V/O South Africa produces 60% of the world’s mohair. 3.8 Million tons of this luxury high end fibre is exported for international clothing brands to Europe, China and Taiwan. Nearly 1000 Angora farms producing mohair are found in a condensed area in the Karoo. A video of angora goats in distress during shearing, is now threatening to close down the industry and put 30 000 people out of a job. Up sound V/O The video was taken on angora farms in January, by an undercover animal rights agent from the UK. It shows goats being dragged across the floor by the legs or the horns; you hear the disturbing sounds of kid goats crying. It becomes simply unbearable to watch. Up sound LINK: The video was produced by a massive animal rights organisation, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or PETA, but now questions are being asked whether the video was ethically produced or indeed accurate. V/O Peta is an international vegan organisation with 6.5 million members, known for its sensational animal anti-cruelty campaigns. South Africa’s mohair industry is its latest target. In 2015 Peta claimed victory after they ran a worldwide campaign against the angora rabbit farms in China. They stated: “Peta has decimated the angora industry! Now let’s win against mohair!” LINK: The story starts in January this year when an Englishman by the name of Joel Hindson knocked on the door of the only estate agent in Steytlerville in the Karoo, posing as a potential buyer of an angora mohair farm. V/O Linda Henderson put Hindson in touch with angora farmers in the area. Linda Henderson: Estate Agent - He reported to be interested in angora goat farming and asked me if I could help him to find his way around farms. He was very particularly interested in the shearing. V/O Sean Hobson is a sixth generation farmer from Jansenville. Sean Hobson: Angora farmer – One of the industry players contacted us and said there is this young man from England who is looking to come to South Africa, buy a farm, start farming goats. V/O During a shearing session Hindson secretly recorded a conversation around the table where Hobson’s father made reference to 40 000 goats that died after a freak weather change in the last century. Peta claimed many goats die of the cold after shearing. Derek Watts: What is the part that is misquoted? Sean Hobson: I was at the shearing table across the table form my dad: Joel was at my left and we were talking about the industry in the eighties, and at one stage there was a massive cold snap that hit the country straight after shearing season and a lot of animals were lost. My dad was talking about a very specific situation that happened 40 odd years ago and this guy quoted that this is something that happens on a regular basis, it’s a lie. V/O Hindson became a familiar face in the area. He visited Fred Colborne from Willowmore during the branding of his goats. Derek Watts: A lot of people are perturbed about the so-called tattooing process, Fred Colborne: Angora farmer - Yeh the tattooing is law in our country and it is done annually once off on a goat at a time. Derek Watts: Would you say there is a lot of suffering? Fred Colborne: No, No, definitely not. If it is done correctly and the goats are handled properly, definitely not a lot of suffering at all. V/O Hindson moved on to Dicky Ogilvy’s farm near Aberdeen. Ogilvy was shearing his goat kids at the time. Derek Watts: Now the bleating of your kids is a big part of the video. How do you explain that? Dicky Ogilvy: Angora farmer - A goat kid by nature, at that age 5,6 months old, they are bleaters of note. Inevitably like any young animal, they are scared. You will find at the second shearing they are dead quiet. Up sound: Vet with Ogilvy looking at sheep with eye problem V/O Macky Hobson is a vet from Graaff-Reinet who was appointed by the mohair industry to look after the welfare of the goats and do farm visits. Derek Watts: It is claimed that the shearing process is incredibly cruel and painful. Macky Hobson: Veterinarian - I totally disagree with that, the shearing process is an absolute necessity for angora goats. If you didn’t shear an angora goat these goats will suffer incredibly if they were not shorn. V/O During Hindson’s visit to Ogilvy’s farm, a sick goat was slaughtered. Peta claimed it was done with a blunt knife. Dicky Ogilvy: That particular case it was a goat that had a cancerous growth on her head, she was in huge discomfort and it was done in such a way as humanly as possible. It was not done with a blunt knife. V/O Peta says that ‘goats who are unprofitable, die agonising deaths’. Farmers say goats are slaughtered only when they have lost their teeth and are unable to eat. Up Peta video; goat being dragged by legs. Derek Watts: What about dragging the goats around by their legs? Mackie Hobson: Look Derek that is not the norm and it is unacceptable and certainly those shearing teams the whole welfare of those shearing teams, those people need to be trained. V/O Shearing is done by outside contractors: OVK is the largest in southern Africa with 900 shearers who pay their workers per goat they shear. Graham Frost manages the shearing teams. Derek Watts: It is a very rushed operation which I guess is tied in with salaries and bonuses, is there not a way to actually give them more time to shear the goats? Graham Frost: Manager Shearing Services OVK - I quite agree they are probably racing for the fact of getting as much money as they can as quickly as they can and I think we must look into it. Derek Watts: We see a shearer actually sitting on a goat? Graham Frost: I am very distressed that that actually happened and we must get to the actual fact what happened. Certainly it is not in our practice to do that. Derek Watts: But in the video we see a goat being pulled by the leg. Graham Frost: It is definitely an issue which I will strictly address with people concerned. V/O Mohair SA, the regulating body for the industry, conducted an internal investigation on the two farms and the OVK shearing teams implicated in the Peta video. OVK said once it has identified the shearers on the video it will suspend their contracts if they are found guilty. The two implicated farmers have been suspended; one of them was Ogilvy. Derek Watts: What were your thoughts when you saw the Peta video? Dicky Ogilvy: I was shocked. Initially I didn't even think this guy could have done this and then having a better look at it I realised I have been implicated here. What went down on that video was edited and narrated in such a way to discredit the entire industry which is grossly unfair. V/O Deon Saayman of Mohair SA is adamant that the scenes depicted in the video is not a true reflection of the mohair industry. Deon Saayman: Managing Director Mohair SA: If you look at these two specific clips these are very isolated incidents Derek. We spent nearly a decade putting sustainable guidelines in place; we have nearly assessed 450 farmers to get on with these practices. V/O An independent investigation by the National SPCA is now in progress. Grace de Lange from the Farm Animal Protection Unit says they will lay charges once they have concluded their findings. Grace de Lange: Manager Farm Animal Protection Unit - We were horrified by some of the things we saw like the dragging of the animals by the legs and horns. So if the shearing company, the farmers and the individuals identified are found guilty of animal cruelty they will face heavy fines, imprisonment, and they will get a criminal record. V/O Hindson visited 12 of the nearly 1000 angora farms in South Africa of which only two were implicated. We called Daniel Paden, Director of Evidence Analysis for PETA in USA. Derek Watts: The point is you have made no attempt to produce a balanced video. You have not gone to anyone in the industry. You have not even gone to vets in this country. Daniel Paden: Director of Evidence Analysis PETA USA: We consulted with no fewer than 6 vets in US and Uk and the consensus there, anonymous, is that what was depicted on that video cause those animals pain and suffering. Derek Watts: Daniel your video is really riddled with inaccuracy, you say that 40 000 goats die a year because of the weather and shearing? Daniel Paden: No the video shows a mohair farmer saying that on one weekend alone 40 000 goats die of exposure in South Africa. Derek Watts: Now the truth there is that goes back to the last century that story and these days the farmers have weather apps to get their goats into enclosures when the weather closes in. Derek Watts: Daniel, what now must happen to almost a million goats around SA? Daniel Paden: My suspicion is that the farmers would probably start to slaughter them in various ways if the demand is going down and they find that they can no longer sell those animals fleeces. V/O On Peta’s website they list over a hundred clothing brands who have joined the boycott against mohair form South Africa: Zara; H&M and Forever 21 is on that list. Derek Watts: What would you say to the world leading brands considering dropping mohair from their ranges? Sean Hobson: We are incredibly proud of our animals. Our animals are our livelihood. Look for the balanced story. Look for the truth out there. __________________________________________________________________________ PROMOS 10 second A video from an animal rights organisation that went viral, threatens to bring down 150 year old mohair industry and put 30 000 people out of a job. 15 second V/O A video by an animal rights organisation of angora goats in distress threatens to close down the mohair industry. Deon Saayman: the first time you see this video, immediately shock, outrage, anger 15 seconds V/O A video of angora goats being apparently treated cruelly threatens to bring down a 150 year old mohair industry. Sean Hobson: Our animals are our livelihood. Look for the balanced story. Look for the truth out there. 30 second V/O A sensational video from an animal rights organisation showing disturbing images of angora goats being shorn for their mohair is threatening to close down the industry and 30 000 people out of a job. Sean Hobson: My life is my goats. It's what i do, it is what my family has done for 6 generations. I can’t accept the fact that a group can shut down my livelihood off a sensationalistic video like that. It's what i do it's my passion. SUNDAY PROMO A video which shows alleged abuse on Angora mohair farms threatens a one hundred and fifty year old industry. Was this animal rights video, fair and balanced? ___________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Peta's Angora video: Truth or fabrication? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche: Angora goats are known for their exotic hair but in a recent video by an animal rights organisation that shocked the world disturbing visuals of goats in distres
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The video, produced by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or Peta, went viral on the 1st of May and since over 100 brands have threatened to stop using mohair in their clothing range. Peta is the largest animal rights organisation in the world with 6.5 million members and supporters. Their top video this month on the angora practices in South Africa, is headlined: “PETA has decimated the angora industry. Now let’s win against mohair!.” In 2015 they destroyed the angora rabbit fur industry in China and their next target was the mohair industry in South Africa. In this 4 minute video produced by Peta they claim “goats are thrown, cut and killed for mohair,” and are calling on a total ban of all mohair products from South Africa. The message resonated strongly as already international brands like Zara, Gap, H&M, Mango, Topshop, Banana Republic, Esprit, Old Navy, Athleta have agreed to take all mohair products off their 2020 winter range. This could spell the end of the mohair industry for South Africa, the potential loss 30 000 jobs and a R1.5 billion rand industry closing down. Peta promotes a total vegan lifestyle and say “animals are not ours to eat, wear, experiment on, use for entertainment or abuse in any way.” They are known to go to extreme lengths to create sensational news and often reported in the media as ‘getting their facts wrong.’ And on every news story where they feed on the emotions of the consumer, the ‘donate’ tab is in bold. Money speaks loudest and rumours has it that their biggest donors are from the oil companies. This has a twofold implication: promoting of synthetic fibres and secondly, an urban myth that the angora farms are smack back in the middle of the Karoo where fracking is said to take place. (our story will not cover these points as that will need far more investigation and possibly a follow up).
metadata.Summary: According to Peta they visited 12 angora farms in the Karoo and “documented pervasive cruelty to animals at every single farm”. “Shearers threw angora goats; cut off swaths of their skin, and cut conscious animals’ throats. Workers picked up goats by the tails, likely breaking them. One farmer dumped rams into tanks of cleaning solution and shoved their heads into the liquid, which he admitted would poison them if they swallowed it.” They continue by saying: “workers punched holes in goats’ ears with pliers, causing the animals to scream. There is no doubt that the visuals are highly disturbing to watch, but look deeper and every single scene has been explained to us in detail by experts on what is standard acceptable procedures and not harmful to the animals in any way as Peta claimed. Par for the one scene where the adult goats are being handled roughly by shearers who were obviously in a hurry to finish, the rest of the scenes are not ‘cruel to animals’ as they claimed. Most consumers have no first hand knowledge of farming practices passed by the NSPCA and independent auditors. Farmers work with strict guidelines on sustainable practices and are controlled by independent organisations like Mohair SA to regulate and monitor farmers. Angora goats are highly sensitive animals and a farmer will go out of his way to ensure that his animal is treated in the best way as this is his ‘bread and butter’.

More information: South Africa produces 60% of the world’s mohair with the remaining 40% produced in Texas, Australia, Lesotho and Spain. 95% of all mohair in the world is processed at factories in Port Elizabeth. Some of the yarn remain here for local products but most is bought by international buyers from Europe and Asia and makes its way to the shelves of top fashion retailers.
